title: Holbrooke Routes Pressure Through Belgrade
sources: General Framework Agreement for Peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina (Dayton, 1995)
ICTY Karadžić Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T), 1995 negotiations findings
content:
When the United States, under the direction of Richard Holbrooke, assembled the diplomatic push that would end the war in late 1995, it made a deliberate procedural choice: it negotiated the Bosnian Serb position through Belgrade rather than directly with the Pale leadership. Slobodan Milošević was given authority to speak for the Bosnian Serbs in the talks that culminated at Dayton. The leadership in Pale, including Radovan Karadžić, by then indicted by the ICTY, was sidelined.

For the Bosnian Serb leadership this was a profound humiliation and a strategic trap. Routing the negotiations through Belgrade confirmed, before the world and in the structure of the peace process itself, that Republika Srpska was a dependency of Serbia rather than a sovereign actor. Milošević, motivated above all by the lifting of sanctions and the salvaging of Serbia’s position, had every incentive to settle on terms the Pale leadership found intolerable — and the authority, as the patron, to do so over their objections. The ICTY Karadžić Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T) recorded the friction this arrangement generated within the Bosnian Serb leadership during the 1995 endgame.

The choice for Pale was whether to accept the Belgrade channel — and with it Milošević’s authority to negotiate away their war aims — or to repudiate the framework and insist that Pale alone spoke for Republika Srpska. The first path led, by way of the General Framework Agreement signed at Dayton, to a settlement that preserved a Serb entity but on terms dictated through the patron. The second meant defying both Belgrade and Washington at the moment the war was being concluded, with no sponsor left to underwrite the defiance.

It was the final iteration of the war’s recurring structural problem for the Bosnian Serbs: the same Belgrade dependence that had armed and sustained the project now held the pen at its conclusion. To comply was to let the patron end the war on the patron’s terms. To defy was to assert a sovereignty the process had already designed out of existence.
